danish.title: Tiende bog (1812) — Kapitel 36
paragraphs: Fyrst Andrejs (fyrst Andrej Bolkonskij) regiment tilhørte reserven, der indtil efter klokken et var stationeret bag Semjonovsk under heftig artilleriild. Hen imod klokken to blev regimentet, der allerede havde mistet over to hundrede mand, rykket frem til en nedtrampet havremark i hullet mellem Semjonovsk og batteriet, det punkt, der den dag blev beskudt af adskillige hundrede fjendtlige kanoner.

Uden at flytte sig fra stedet eller fyre et eneste skud mistede regimentet her endnu en tredjedel af sine folk. Forfra og især fra højre, i den uafbrudte røg, drønede kanonerne, og ud af røgens mystiske sfære, der dækkede hele rummet foran dem, kom hurtige, hvislende kanonkugler og langsomme, dybe granater. Nogle gange, som for at give dem en pause, gik der et kvarters tid, hvor alle skud fløj forbi, men så faldt fire eller fem mand inden for ét minut, og gang på gang blev de døde slæbt væk og de sårede båret bort.

For hvert nyt nedslag svandt udsigten til at slippe levende derfra for dem, der endnu var i live. Regimentets bataljoner stod i kolonner med tre hundrede skridts mellemrum, men stemningen var den samme overalt. Alle var tavse og mørke. Kun sjældent talte nogen i geledderne, og hver gang de hørte det dumpe stød af en kugle, der ramte, og råbet: »Bårer!«, forstummede samtalen helt. Det meste af tiden sad soldaterne på jorden efter officerernes ordre. En havde taget sin chakot af og sad omhyggeligt og løsnede rynkerne i foret og trak dem til igen. En anden gned tørt ler mellem håndfladerne og pudsede sin bajonet med det. En tredje pillede ved remmen og trak i spændet på sit bandoler. En fjerde glattede sine benvikler, lagde dem om på ny og trak støvlerne på. Nogle byggede små huse af jordknolde fra pløjemarken eller flettede kurve af strå ude i kornet. Alle så ud til at gå helt op i deres gøremål. At mænd faldt døde eller sårede om, at båre efter båre blev båret forbi, at tropper trak sig tilbage, at store fjendtlige styrker kom til syne gennem røgen, det ænsede ingen. Men rykkede vores artilleri eller kavaleri frem, eller så de noget af vores infanteri gå frem, lød der opmuntrende tilråb fra alle sider. Det, der vakte den livligste interesse, var dog ting, som slet ingen forbindelse havde med slaget. Det var, som om disse mænd var så udslidte på sjælen, at de fandt lindring i det mest dagligdags. Et batteri kørte forbi foran regimentet. En af hestene for en ammunitionsvogn fik benet over skaglen. »Hov, se lige den hest! Få benet fri! Nu falder den … Åh, de ser det ikke!« Nøjagtig de samme råb lød langs hele regimentets front. En anden gang samlede al interesse sig om en lille brun hund, der kom, Gud ved hvorfra, og travede forbi geledderne, optaget af sit eget og med halen stift i vejret. Pludselig slog en granat ned lige ved siden af den. Hunden gav et hyl, stak halen mellem benene og fór til siden. Hele regimentet skreg af grin. Men det var kun et øjebliks adspredelse. I otte timer havde mændene siddet uvirksomme, uden mad og i stadig dødsangst, og deres blege, dystre ansigter blev blegere og dystrere.

Bleg og dyster som alle andre i regimentet gik fyrst Andrej frem og tilbage fra det ene markskel til det andet i udkanten af engen langs en havremark, med bøjet hoved og hænderne på ryggen. Han havde intet at bestille, ingen ordrer at give. Alt gik af sig selv. De døde blev slæbt bort fra forreste række, de sårede båret væk, og geledderne sluttede sig. Løb en soldat bagud, var han i en fart tilbage igen. I begyndelsen var fyrst Andrej gået rundt i rækkerne. Han anså det for sin pligt at sætte mod i folkene og vise dem et eksempel. Men snart indså han, at det var overflødigt. Han kunne ingenting lære dem. Uden at vide af det brugte han, som hver eneste soldat dér, alle sine sjælekræfter på at holde tanken om deres frygtelige stilling fra livet. Han slæbte fødderne hen over engen, så græsset raslede, og så på støvet på sine støvler. Snart tog han lange skridt for at træde i høstfolkenes fodspor, snart talte han sine skridt og regnede ud, hvor mange gange han skulle gå fra det ene skel til det andet for at tilbagelægge en mil. Så plukkede han blomsterne af den malurt, der groede i furen langs skellet, gned dem mellem hænderne og indåndede deres skarpe, bittersøde duft. Af gårsdagens tanker var der intet tilbage. Han tænkte ikke på noget. Med trætte ører lyttede han til de bestandig tilbagevendende lyde, skelnede projektilernes piben fra skuddenes drøn, kastede et blik på de alt for velkendte ansigter i første bataljon og ventede. »Der kommer den … nu er der én på vej herhen igen!« tænkte han, mens han lyttede til en piben, der nærmede sig derude fra det skjulte land af røg. »Én til! Og én til! Igen! Den ramte …« Han standsede og så hen mod geledderne. »Nej, den gik over. Men den her ramte!« Så gav han sig igen til at prøve, om han kunne nå skellet med seksten skridt. En susen, et bump! Fem skridt fra ham flåede en kanonkugle den tørre jord op og forsvandt. Det løb ham koldt ned ad ryggen. Igen så han hen mod geledderne. Der var nok mange, der var ramt: ved anden bataljon havde en stor flok samlet sig.
»Adjudant!« råbte han. »Sig dem, at de ikke skal klumpe sig sammen.«
Adjudanten adlød ordren og nærmede sig fyrst Andrej. Fra den modsatte side red en bataljonskommandør hen.

»Pas på!« lød et forskrækket råb fra en soldat, og som en fugl, der svirrer i hurtig flugt og slår ned på jorden, faldt en granat med et sagte sus ned to skridt fra fyrst Andrej og tæt på bataljonskommandørens hest. Hesten — uden at spørge, om det var rigtigt eller forkert at vise frygt — stejlede, snerrede og sprang til side, næsten kastende rytteren af. Hesten galoperede bort over marken.
»Læg jer ned!« råbte adjudanten og kastede sig fladt på jorden.
Fyrst Andrej stod og tøvede. Granaten drejede rundt som en snurretop mellem ham og den udstrakte adjudant, nær en malurtplante mellem marken og engen.

»Kan dette virkelig være døden?« tænkte fyrst Andrej og kiggede med et helt nyt, misundeligt blik på græsset, malurten og den smalle røgstribe, der steg op fra den roterende sorte kugle. »Jeg kan ikke, jeg vil ikke dø. Jeg elsker livet — jeg elsker dette græs, denne jord, denne luft...« Han tænkte dette, og i samme øjeblik huskede han, at folk kiggede på ham.
»Det er en skam, hr. adjudant!« sagde han til adjudanten. »Hvad...«

Han nåede ikke at tale færdigt. Samtidig lød en eksplosion, en hvinen af splinter som fra en knust vinduesramme, en kvælende lugt af krudt, og fyrst Andrej kastede sig til den ene side, løftede armen og faldt om på brystet. Flere officerer løb hen til ham. Fra højre side af maven sivede en stor plet blod ud over græsset.
Militsmændene med bårer, der var tilkaldt, stod bag officererne. Fyrst Andrej lå på brystet med ansigtet i græsset og åndede tungt og støjende.
»Hvad venter I på? Kom!«
Bønderne gik hen og greb ham ved skuldrene og benene, men han jamrede ynkeligt, og de satte ham ned igen efter at have vekslet blikke.
»Tag ham op, løft ham, det gør ingen forskel!« råbte nogen.
De greb ham igen ved skuldrene og lagde ham på båren.
»Åh, Gud! Min Gud! Hvad er det? Maven? Så er det døden! Min Gud!« — hørtes der stemmer bland officererne.
»Den fløj en hårsbred forbi mit øre,« sagde adjudanten.
Bønderne justerede båren på deres skuldre og begyndte hastigt at gå ad den sti, de havde trådt ned, mod forbindingspladsen.
»Hold trit! Nå, de bønder!« råbte en officer og greb bønderne i skuldrene for at standse dem, da de gik ujævnt og rystede båren.
»Gå i takt, Fjodor... hører du, Fjodor!« sagde den forreste bonde.
»Nå, det er bedre!« sagde den bageste glad, da han var kommet i takt.
»Deres Excellence! Fyrste!« sagde Timokhins (kaptajn Timokhin) rystende stemme; han var løbet hen og kiggede ned på båren.
Fyrst Andrej åbnede øjnene og kiggede op fra båren, hvor hans hoved lå sunket dybt ned, på den, der talte, og hans øjenlåg faldt til igen.

Militsfolkene bar fyrst Andrej hen til forbindingspladsen ved skoven, hvor vognene holdt. Tre telte med teltdugene slået til side var rejst i udkanten af en birkeskov. Inde mellem træerne stod vogne og heste. Hestene åd havre af deres løse krybber, og spurve slog ned og hakkede de korn i sig, som faldt på jorden. Nogle krager havde fået færten af blod og fløj utålmodigt skræppende mellem birkene. Omkring teltene, over et område på mere end to hektar, stod og sad og lå blodige mænd i alle slags klæder. Rundt om de sårede flokkedes bårebærerne med dystre, opmærksomme ansigter. Officererne, der skulle holde orden, forsøgte forgæves at jage dem væk. Soldaterne ænsede ikke ordrerne. De støttede sig til bårerne og stirrede ufravendt på det, der foregik for øjnene af dem, som prøvede de at løse en vanskelig gåde. Inde fra teltene lød snart høje, vrede råb, snart en klynkende stønnen. Af og til kom en sygehjælper løbende ud for at hente vand eller pege på den næste, der skulle bæres ind. De sårede, der ventede udenfor på deres tur, stønnede, sukkede, græd, skreg, bandede eller bad om vodka. Nogle talte i vildelse. De mænd, der bar fyrst Andrej, skrævede hen over de sårede, som endnu ikke var blevet forbundet. Da han var regimentschef, bar de ham helt hen til et af teltene. Der standsede de og ventede på besked. Fyrst Andrej slog øjnene op. Længe kunne han ikke forstå, hvad der foregik omkring ham. Han huskede engen, malurten, marken, den snurrende sorte kugle og den lidenskabelige kærlighed til livet, der pludselig var vældet op i ham. To skridt fra ham stod en høj, smuk, sorthåret underofficer med hovedet i bind. Han støttede sig til en gren og talte så højt, at alle lagde mærke til ham. Han var ramt af geværkugler i hovedet og benet. Omkring ham stod en flok sårede og bårebærere og lyttede ivrigt.

»Vi sparkede dem ud derfra, så han måtte slippe alt, og vi fangede kongen selv!« råbte en soldat med glimtende feberinfiltrerede øjne. »Bare der var kommet forstærkninger lige på det tidspunkt, drenge, så havde der slet ikke været noget tilbage af ham! Det siger jeg for sikkert...«

Ligesom alle andre nær den talende kiggede fyrst Andrej på ham med skinnende øjne og oplevede en følelse af trøst. »Men er det ikke alt lige meget nu?« tænkte han. »Og hvad venter mig derhenne, og hvad har der været her? Hvorfor var jeg så uvillig til at skille mig fra livet? Der var noget i dette liv, som jeg ikke forstod og stadig ikke forstår.«

english.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 36
paragraphs: Prince Andrew's regiment was among the reserves that until after one o'clock were stationed idle behind Semenovsk under heavy artillery fire. Toward two o'clock the regiment, having already lost over two hundred men, was moved forward into a trampled oat field in the gap between Semenovsk and the Knoll Battery — where thousands perished that day — and onto which an intense, concentrated fire from several hundred enemy guns was directed between one and two o'clock.

Without moving from that spot or firing a single shot, the regiment lost another third of its men. From the front, and especially from the right, guns boomed ceaselessly through the ever-present smoke, and from that mysterious shroud of smoke that covered the whole forward space, quick hissing cannonballs and slow whistling shells flew without pause. At times, as if to grant them a reprieve, a quarter of an hour would pass during which all the projectiles sailed overhead, but sometimes several men were torn from the regiment in a single minute, and the dead were constantly dragged away and the wounded carried off.

With each fresh blow, the chances of survival for those still standing grew slimmer. The regiment stood in battalion columns three hundred paces apart, but all the men shared the same mood — taciturn and somber. Talk was rare in the ranks and ceased altogether each time the thud of a successful hit was heard with the cry "Stretchers!" Most of the time, on their officers' orders, the men sat on the ground. One, having removed his cap, carefully adjusted and tightened its lining; another rubbed dry clay between his palms to polish his bayonet; another fingered his belt strap and tugged at its buckle; another smoothed and refolded his leg wrappings and put his boots back on. Some built little houses from clods of plowed earth, or braided baskets from the straw in the field. All seemed entirely absorbed in these tasks. When men were killed or wounded, when rows of stretchers passed, when troops fell back, or when great masses of the enemy came into view through the smoke, no one paid any attention. But when their own artillery or cavalry advanced, or their own infantry was seen moving forward, approving shouts were heard on all sides. Yet the liveliest interest was drawn to events completely unrelated to the battle — as if the minds of these morally exhausted men found relief in everyday, ordinary things. An artillery battery was passing in front of the regiment. A horse from an ammunition cart got its leg caught over a trace. "Hey, look at that trace horse! Get her leg out! She'll fall! They can't see it!" — the same cries rang out from every part of the regiment. Another time, a small brown dog of unknown origin trotted purposefully in front of the ranks with its tail stiffly upright, until suddenly a shell landed nearby, and it yelped, tucked its tail between its legs, and bolted sideways. Howls and shrieks of laughter erupted across the whole regiment. But such distractions lasted only a moment, and for eight hours the men had been idle, without food, in constant fear of death, and their pale, gloomy faces grew ever paler and gloomier.

Prince Andrew, as pale and grim as everyone else in the regiment, paced back and forth along the edge of the meadow beside the oat field, head bowed, hands clasped behind his back. There was nothing for him to do and no orders to give. Everything went on by itself. The killed were dragged from the front, the wounded carried away, the ranks closed up. If any soldiers ran to the rear, they returned immediately. At first Prince Andrew, considering it his duty to inspire courage, walked among the ranks, but he soon realized this was unnecessary — there was nothing he could teach them. All the powers of his soul, like every soldier's there, were unconsciously focused on avoiding contemplation of the horror of their situation. He walked along the meadow, dragging his feet through the grass and watching the dust on his boots; now he took long strides trying to step in the mowers' footprints; now he counted his steps, calculating how many trips between one strip and another would make a mile; now he plucked wormwood flowers growing along a boundary ditch, crushed them in his palms, and inhaled their sharp, bittersweet scent. Nothing remained of the previous day's thoughts. He thought of nothing. He listened with tired ears to the same recurring sounds, distinguishing the whistle of flying shells from the boom of cannon reports, and glanced at the wearyingly familiar faces of the first battalion's men, and waited. "Here it comes — this one's heading our way again!" he thought, listening to the approaching whistle from the hidden region of smoke. "One, another! Again! It hit..." He stopped and looked at the ranks. "No, it went over. But this one hit!" And again he started trying to reach the boundary strip in sixteen paces. A whizz and a thud! Five paces away, a cannonball tore up the dry earth and disappeared. A chill ran down his back. Again he glanced at the ranks. Probably many had been hit — a large crowd had gathered near the second battalion.
"Adjutant!" he shouted. "Order them not to bunch up."
The adjutant, having carried out the order, approached Prince Andrew. From the other direction, a battalion commander rode up.

"Look out!" came a frightened cry from a soldier, and like a bird whirring in rapid flight and landing on the ground, a shell dropped with little noise within two steps of Prince Andrew and close to the battalion commander's horse. The horse — caring nothing about right or wrong in showing fear — snorted, reared, nearly threw the major, and bolted aside. Its terror infected the men.
"Lie down!" cried the adjutant, throwing himself flat.
Prince Andrew hesitated. The smoking shell spun like a top between him and the prostrate adjutant, near a wormwood plant between the field and the meadow.

"Can this be death?" thought Prince Andrew, gazing with entirely new, envious eyes at the grass, the wormwood, and the thread of smoke curling from the spinning black ball. "I cannot — I do not wish to die. I love life — I love this grass, this earth, this air..." He thought this, and at the same time remembered that people were watching him.
"It's shameful, sir!" he said to the adjutant. "What..."

He didn't finish. Simultaneously came the sound of an explosion, a whistle of splinters like a window frame shattering, a suffocating smell of powder, and Prince Andrew lurched to one side, flung up his arm, and fell on his chest. Several officers ran to him. From the right side of his abdomen, blood was pouring out, forming a large stain on the grass.
The militiamen with stretchers who were called up stood behind the officers. Prince Andrew lay on his chest with his face in the grass, breathing heavily and noisily.
"What are you waiting for? Come on!"
The peasants went up and took him by the shoulders and legs, but he moaned so pitifully that, exchanging glances, they set him down again.
"Pick him up — lift him — it's all the same!" someone cried.
They took him by the shoulders again and laid him on the stretcher.
"Oh God! My God! What is it? The stomach? That means death! My God!" — voices among the officers could be heard saying.
"It flew a hair's breadth past my ear," said the adjutant.
The peasants, adjusting the stretcher to their shoulders, started hurriedly along the path they had worn to the dressing station.
"Keep in step! Those peasants!" shouted an officer, grabbing the peasants by their shoulders to steady them as they walked unevenly, jolting the stretcher.
"Get in step, Fyodor — I mean it, Fyodor!" said the lead peasant.
"That's right!" said the one behind joyfully when he'd matched the step.
"Your excellency! Prince!" said the trembling voice of Timokhin, who had run up and was looking down at the stretcher.
Prince Andrew opened his eyes and looked up from the stretcher, into which his head had sunk deep, then closed them again.

The militiamen carried Prince Andrew to the dressing station at the edge of the wood, where wagons were parked. The station consisted of three tents with their flaps turned back, pitched beside a birch wood. In the wood, wagons and horses stood; the horses were eating oats from their portable troughs, and sparrows flew down to peck at fallen grains. Crows, drawn by the scent of blood, flew among the birch trees, cawing impatiently. Around the tents, over an area of more than five acres, bloodstained men in various uniforms stood, sat, or lay. Crowds of soldier stretcher-bearers with grim, attentive faces stood around the wounded, and the officers trying to keep order couldn't drive them away. Ignoring the officers' commands, the soldiers leaned on their stretchers and stared intently, as if trying to comprehend the difficult problem of what was happening before them. From the tents came now loud, angry cries, now pitiful groans. Occasionally attendants ran out to fetch water or to point out who should be brought in next. The wounded waiting their turn outside the tents groaned, sighed, wept, screamed, cursed, or begged for vodka. Some were delirious. Prince Andrew's bearers, stepping over the unbandaged wounded, carried him — as a regimental commander — close to one of the tents and stopped there, awaiting instructions. Prince Andrew opened his eyes and for a long time couldn't make out what was going on around him. He remembered the meadow, the wormwood, the field, the spinning black ball, and his sudden, passionate rush of love for life. Two steps away, leaning against a branch and talking loudly — drawing everyone's attention — stood a tall, handsome, dark-haired noncommissioned officer with a bandaged head. He'd been wounded in the head and leg by bullets. Around him, listening eagerly, a crowd of wounded men and stretcher-bearers had gathered.

"We kicked him out of there so hard he dropped everything — we grabbed the King himself!" the man cried, his feverish eyes glittering. "If only reserves had come up just then, boys — there wouldn't have been anything left of him! I'm telling you for sure..."

Like all the others near the speaker, Prince Andrew looked at him with shining eyes and felt a sense of comfort. "But isn't it all the same now?" he thought. "And what will be there, and what has there been here? Why was I so reluctant to let go of life? There was something in this life I did not, and do not, understand."
